## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, choosing who asks my questions is an obvious last setup step, and it comes naturally after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question and the hint are clear on first reading: an AI interviewer on video, typing or tapping as an alternative, a preselected voice, 400 credits and a text-message link.
screens.why3: I can play the 5-second samples and decide which voice my reservation agents would listen to, so this needs no knowledge beyond my own judgement.
screens.why4: Two distinct named voices, each with a sample and one already preselected, are a complete choice, and no escape chip is needed because the default covers having no preference.
screens.why5: It keeps my actor, reservation agents, says who will be asked, and changes nothing about my idea.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, it is obvious why Keel wants to know how my reservation agents will answer.
screens.why2: I can pick on first reading, but the Daphne option is wordy and "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" and "Ready when Daphne is" take a second read to see that they mean her video is still being prepared.
screens.why3: I know my agents work on shift between calls and at a busy desk, so I can judge whether talking to a video or reading and tapping suits them.
screens.why4: AI video, read and tap, or letting them choose covers the real choices, and the three are distinct, with the "more than 9 in 10 where it is loud" figure useful for a noisy front desk.
screens.why5: It keeps my "reservation agents" and my pick of "Read and tap" is there as offered, with nothing changing what I typed about Codyco.

screens.why1: Having settled the questions, the pilot and how agents answer, the last thing to decide before sending is who receives the link, so it clearly belongs here at the end.
screens.why2: The question and all three options are plain to me on first read, though 'the Contacts page' assumes I know a part of Keel, and the option text explains it well enough.
screens.why3: I know how I can reach reservation agents, whether through the hotel groups we already work with, a search or a trade group, so I can answer this from my own situation.
screens.why4: Named people, people found through Keel and an open group link are distinct and cover the ways I would reach agents, and each option says what happens to the link.
screens.why5: The screen does not change anything I typed and my pick of people I know by name is offered as written, with no drift in my idea or roles.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title and each card carries its deciding count against its bar (6 of 7, 5 of 7 at the bar, 6 of 7), with the rule that the verdict is the worst card tying them together.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on the stage page, but each card's count line says what was counted, over 7, and where the bar sits, though "5 of 7 said it would have gone better, 5 of them a lot" and the tally "3 holding" take a second look.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are word for word the ones I checked on the way in, even though the garbled statement above them is not how I would say it.
screens.why_b4: The page never says what this means for Codyco or what to do next, such as whether to move on to the pilot or look at the three who set a condition on letting the AI answer.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and "at the bar" and "3 on a condition" are honest, but nothing says 7 is a small group, and "Holding up" for the whole solution softly overstates a result where relative advantage sits exactly on the bar and half the adoption yeses are conditional.
screens.instead: Holding up, narrowly, among only 7 people: forwarding is fine, but relative advantage only just reaches the bar and 3 of the 6 who would let the AI answer set a condition, so read those conditions before you sell the €3,000 pilot.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so I have both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The four answer options are counted and marked for or against, the strip shows 6 for and 1 against across 7 people, and the marker sits at 5, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The name Compatibility and the line about forwarding unanswered calls to another number are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me concretely that forwarding is not the blocker and that I should look at adoption friction next.
screens.why_b5: The count line shows n=7 and says "a lean, not a call", but the So line flatly says forwarding will not stop them and adoption friction will, which is more than 7 people can carry and passes over Aylin's phone system that needs IT and an owner who won't pay.
screens.instead: Among these 7, forwarding doesn't look like the main blocker, though one old phone system would need IT and the owner's money; adoption friction, below, looks like the bigger risk.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside the deciding number, 5 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, and it says plainly that I am at the bar.
screens.why_b2: The count over 7 people and the bar are plain, but the bar is said two ways (5 of 7 for, no more than 1 in 3 against) and "Better · 5 5 a lot · 0 a little" takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and "missed calls turned into bookings" are exactly the name and line I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and points me to Adoption friction, so it does not say what being exactly at the bar means for the idea or what to do about Chiara's covered phones and Tobias's refusal.
screens.why_b5: It keeps 7 in view, calls it "a lean, not a call", flags the answers as hypothetical and says "imagined", so nothing claims more than these people can carry.
screens.instead: 5 of 7 imagined their last shift going better, all 5 a lot, which just reaches your bar with no room to spare: one more no would drop it; the 2 against are a call center already covering the phones and an agent who won't hand guests to a machine, so test next whether groups with after-hours cover still see the gain and read Adoption friction below.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly beside the deciding number, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know my belief held and on what count.
screens.why_b2: The four answer choices, their counts adding to 7, and the marker at 5 of 7 show what is counted, over how many people, and where the bar sits at first look.
screens.why_b3: The Adoption friction title and the belief line are exactly what I checked, and although "You said let an AI answer..." reads as a clumsy fragment, it is still my belief in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line points me to what would make it worth it to the 3 conditional agents, but only names and answer labels follow, so I still don't know what to prove to them or how to handle Tobias's no.
screens.why_b5: The 3 conditional yeses are stated beside the 6 of 7, all 7 answers are listed, and the screen says "a small group: a lean, not a call", so it makes no claim beyond these people.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only 3 of 7 would let the AI answer as is; show what each of the 3 conditional agents needs to see and why Tobias said no, then tell me to prove that before the pilot.

screens.why_b1: Each box states the verdict beside its deciding number ("Holding up", "6 of 7", "bar 5 of 7"), and the line under the question repeats it ("held, 5 of 7"), so I know the answer and can see why from the people against.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Relative advantage are the names I checked, and the belief lines about forwarding unanswered calls and the last shift going better are word for word what I confirmed.
screens.why_b4: The screen stops at the verdicts and quotes, so it never says what they mean for me, such as qualifying out groups whose call center already covers after hours or checking old phone systems before a pilot.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and nothing is claimed beyond the 7, but "the 1 who said no" and "the 2 who said no" flatten "Only sometimes" and "No difference" into a no, the "held, 5 of 7" line drops the "at the bar" caveat, and nothing says 7 is a small sample.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: the owner who won't pay to replace a phone system that can't forward, guests who ring for a person who knows the house, and an agent whose call center covers after six and whose real pain is group requests and emails with no rates.

screens.why1: As the first question in a study about my work, it makes sense to check straight away whether I work in the kind of place the study is about.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call center are everyday words in my job, so I can answer on first reading, though in Germany I would say call centre or Callcenter without any trouble.
screens.why3: I work in our group's central reservations office in Munich, so I know this for certain without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a screener rightly has no escape chip because I either work at such a group or I don't.
screens.why5: It names only my kind of workplace and nothing about a product, a plan or what the founder calls people like me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with no parenthesis or abbreviation, at 17 words, and yes or no is easy to hold after hearing it once.

screens.why1: Right after asking if I work at such an office, it makes sense to check whether I actually took calls recently before asking for a story.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, and I understand it at once.
screens.why3: I take booking calls on every shift, so I know this without having to think.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but two escape chips is one too many, and 'I can't recall one particular shift' is odd because nobody forgets whether calls came in this week.
screens.why5: It stays on booking calls during my shift, with nothing about a product or company leaking to me, and it keeps the founder's meaning.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is short, a single question, and ends in a simple yes or no with no escape read out.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you take a booking call on your shift? Yes / No

screens.why1: After being asked whether booking calls come in on my shift, it makes sense that Part 2 now shows me an idea about the calls nobody picks up.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot, Apaleo, forwarding calls and the desk are my everyday words, so I understand the card on first reading, though *in the hotel's voice* is a little loose.
screens.why3: I handle these calls and write bookings into the PMS every shift, so I can judge from my own work what this would do with missed calls.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read and shows no options.
screens.why5: It is an idea card shown on purpose, and it keeps a clear meaning in terms I use, with nothing about the founder's plan or labels for people leaking to me.
screens.why6: It says well in short sentences, but it is long to hold in one hearing, *PMS* is spoken as letters, the list of three system names is a mouthful, and the belief repeats the how instead of pointing back to it.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI phone agent for the calls nobody picks up. Your hotel forwards those calls to it; it answers the guest's questions, takes the payment and writes the confirmed booking into your PMS, and it hands a call to the desk by rules the hotel sets. The people building it believe this would turn those missed calls into bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea about unanswered calls, it is obvious why they ask whether my missed calls could be sent to another number.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, but "could you" leaves me unsure whether it means I am allowed to, whether our phone system can do it, or whether I would do it during a call rush.
screens.why3: I work the phones in the central office every shift, so I know whether our system lets calls be forwarded or whether that is set up by IT.
screens.why4: The range works and I can't tell fits, but "most of the time" and "only sometimes" fit a setting that is available or not less well, and there is no clean option for "only IT or my supervisor can set that".
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose, the question stays on the plain act of forwarding calls, and nothing of the product's workings or founder's terms leaks in.
screens.why6: It is two short sentences with one question and four short options I can hold after one hearing, and the escape comes last.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. Could unanswered calls on your line be forwarded to another number? Yes, I could do it myself; Yes, but IT or a supervisor would have to set it; No; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after hearing the idea and whether I could forward calls, it makes sense to ask if this would have helped on my last shift.
screens.why2: I understand it on first reading: would this thing have made my last shift better, yes or no, and how much.
screens.why3: I know how my last shift went and which calls we missed, but the card tells me so little about how Codyco works that I would partly be guessing at the effect.
screens.why4: The scale from a lot better through no difference to worse covers every answer, the options are distinct and plain, and I can't tell fits someone who only knows one line about the product.
screens.why5: The product appears only on the idea card and in a question about that idea, and confirmed bookings from unanswered calls stays true to the job of turning callers into bookings without any insider terms reaching me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold after one hearing, and the escape comes last as a short phrase.

screens.why1: After the idea and whether it would have helped my shift, it makes sense to ask whether I would actually let an AI answer our guests.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, but "in your hotel's voice" could mean our greeting and tone or a copied voice, and I would need a second to settle that.
screens.why3: I know how I feel about an AI taking guest calls and can answer that, but as a reservation agent I would not be the one to decide it for the hotel group, so "let" is partly a guess at a power I do not have.
screens.why4: The scale covers my likely answers and the escape fits, but "Yes, if it was clearly worth it" is vague and could be said of almost anything, and it does not offer the condition I would really name, such as only after hours or when no agent is free.
screens.why5: It is the idea card's own product and plainly the thing I am being asked about, with no founder jargon or talk of roles reaching me beyond what the idea shows.
screens.why6: It is short and says well, with one question and four brief options I can hold after one hearing, then a single escape.
screens.instead: Would you be okay with an AI answering the calls nobody at your hotel can pick up, or not? Yes; Yes, but only after hours or at peak; Probably not; or No. Or say I can't tell.
